## Nigeria, 1979 {.hook}

> **A 31-year-old Swiss entomologist arrives in West Africa for a new
> job. He walks straight into a crisis that threatens famine for
> tens of millions of people. What is it — and what does he do about
> it?**
>
> *Un entomologiste suisse de 31 ans arrive en Afrique de l'Ouest pour
> un nouveau poste. Il tombe en plein milieu d'une crise qui menace
> la famine pour des dizaines de millions de personnes. Qu'est-ce que
> c'est — et que fait-il ?*

::: {.notes}
Let guesses land before the reveal. ~1.5 min including setup.

## Cassava feeds hundreds of millions

- Cassava (*Manihot esculenta*) is a staple crop across much of
  sub-Saharan Africa — calorie-dense, drought-tolerant, grows in
  poor soil
- In the early 1970s, a new pest appears: the **cassava mealybug**
  (*Phenacoccus manihoti*), accidentally introduced from South
  America
- Africa's cassava had **never evolved with this insect** — by the
  late 1970s, yield losses of up to 80% in some regions, and a
  famine threat across the entire cassava belt

::: {.notes}
~1.5 min. Direct structural echo of Week 3's phylloxera story: a
naive host (African cassava) meets a well-adapted invasive pest with
zero coevolutionary history behind it.
:::

## Hans Rudolf Herren's idea

- Herren, at the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture
  (IITA, Nigeria), reasons: if the mealybug is from South America,
  its **natural enemies** should be there too
- He searches Central and South America for an insect that
  specifically controls the mealybug back home
- He finds a tiny parasitoid wasp, **_Anagyrus lopezi_**, native to
  Paraguay, that lays its eggs inside mealybugs

::: {.notes}
~1.5 min. This is classical biological control: instead of
engineering the plant's own defense (last week's whole topic), import
the pest's own enemy from its native range.
:::

## The release — and the outcome

- *Anagyrus lopezi* is mass-reared and released across the African
  cassava belt starting in 1981 — one of the largest classical
  biological control efforts ever attempted
- The wasp establishes and spreads **on its own**, tracking the
  mealybug across the continent without further human help
- Within about a decade, the mealybug is permanently suppressed —
  an estimated **20+ million lives** saved from famine; Herren
  receives the 1995 World Food Prize

**Bridge to today: Herren didn't make cassava fight back directly —
he recruited a third party to do the fighting. That's exactly what
plants do too, every day, with chemistry instead of airplanes.**

::: {.notes}
~2 min close. Explicit bridge into "indirect resistance" / tritrophic
interactions: recruiting a natural enemy of the herbivore, rather
than resisting the herbivore directly, is this week's whole theme -
Herren's program is a human-engineered version of exactly what
HIPV-signaling plants do chemically later in this lecture.
Source: Herren, H.R. and Neuenschwander, P. (1991). Biological
control of cassava pests in Africa. Annual Review of Entomology.
:::
